newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JOHNSONS SPLIT OVER WILD CARD INVITATIONS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSONS SPLIT OVER WILD CARD INVITATIONS.

text.p: Michael Johnson made his first public appearance of the world championships at a sweltering nightclub on Thursday and defended the wild card invitation which gave him a backdoor entry.
Johnson, the Olympic 200 and 400 metres champion, looked set to miss the event after injury forced him out of the United States trials in June.

That cost him his place in the U.S. team, but the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), eager to have as many of elite athletes competing as possible, controversially instigated a late rule change earlier this month giving defending champions the automatic right to defend their titles.
Johnson, who has the highest profile of any of the wild card entrants, said he was delighted to take part.
"It's good for me as I didn't think I was going to be here after missing the trials because I was injured but now I am healthy," he said.
"It's good for the other athletes who did not get a chance to compete at the trials and it's good for the IAAF. It gives them a guarantee that they are going to have a good field in each event.
"The best athletes are going to be competing, most of the reigning world champions are going to be here and I think it's good for the public, the sponsors and I'm very pleased it's happened."

Johnson, speaking during a brief stage-managed news conference organised by his shoe sponsors, also said he had recovered from the quadriceps injury he suffered during his head-to-head 150 metres race against Donovan Bailey in Toronto two months ago.
As Johnson talked, his interviewer was visibly wilting under the hot TV arc-lights that illuminated the stage.
And as the temperature continued to rise in the Bad Wolf nightclub while lamb, chicken and meat kebabs sizzled on mini-stoves, Johnson was hustled away out of a side-entrance.
Not everyone agreed with his sentiments.
Allen Johnson, the world and Olympic 110 hurdles champion, stayed as cool as he could in a darkened alcove and offered a different perspective.
Allen, no relation to Michael, said: "I have mixed views on the wildcard. I think it's a good idea but they did it too quickly.
"Change is necessary for progress but I think the choice the IAAF made about the wildcard this year was an emotional decision. Nobody thought anything about it until Michael Johnson got hurt.

"That's not to say that because he got hurt they should not have thought about the idea. I just don't think it should have happened as quickly as it did. I don't think the IAAF has taken enough time to take into consideration the effect this is going to have on each country.
"Because now, as it stands the stars don't have to go to the national championship and so what are the national federations going to do about that?"
